title: The energy transition
subtitle: Towards carbon neutrality
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: The world is trying to replace fossil fuels with cleaner sources. A change as necessary as it is difficult.

hero.hook: Solar power has become the cheapest energy in history. All that remains is to store it.

blocks.text: For a long time, humanity changed energy sources by choice of efficiency: from wood to coal, then from coal to oil. The current **energy transition** is different: for the first time, it is imposed by a survival constraint, climate change.
This course explores how the world is trying to replace fossil fuels with cleaner sources, and why this shift is as difficult as it is necessary.

The framework that guides all energy policies today is called the , signed in 2015. This treaty commits the countries of the world to limit global warming, with a specific objective: to remain if possible below 1.5°C above levels before the industrial era. Every additional tenth of a degree makes extreme weather events worse. **[[Paris Agreement (2015) and climate goals]]**

blocks.caption: Solar panels and wind turbines symbolize the world's shift towards low-carbon energy sources.

blocks.text: To meet this objective, States aim for : a balance between greenhouse gases emitted by human activities and their absorption by forests, soils, oceans, or capture technologies. This assumes that global emissions stop increasing before 2025, then fall sharply in subsequent years. **[[carbon neutrality]]**

The cost of solar power fell 90% between 2010 and 2020, a faster decline than almost any other technology in economic history. In 2023, solar power will even become the cheapest source of electricity ever produced in many parts of the world.

The main driver of the transition is economic. Photovoltaic solar ****, formerly reserved for satellites, has seen its price divided by ten in fifteen years, thanks to technical progress and economies of scale. **Z**, particularly installed at sea where the winds are stronger and more regular, has also reached real industrial maturity. In 2023, almost 90% of new electricity capacity installed worldwide will already come from renewable energies.

A major challenge remains: solar and wind power suffer from **intermittent**, that is to say they do not produce electricity continuously. Hence the importance of large capacity batteries, the price of which has followed the same spectacular fall as that of solar, making electric cars increasingly competitive.

China now manufactures more than 80% of the world's solar panels and more than 70% of lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles. The West's energy transition therefore depends largely on a Chinese manufacturing chain.

sections.title: New obstacles: storage and rare metals

blocks.text: Despite this enthusiasm, the transition faces very real limits. Unlike gas or coal, which can be burned at will, renewable energies require more flexible electricity networks, with storage or backup sources such as hydrogen or nuclear power.

Another obstacle is the shift from a dependence on oil to a dependence on  and other metals, such as lithium or cobalt, needed to make batteries and wind turbines. China controls a huge share of global refining of these materials, creating new vulnerabilities for Europe and the United States. **[[rare earths]]**

Finally, the transition encounters social resistance: fossil fuel industries still employ millions of people, and transforming these jobs without destroying them is an essential condition for the transition to be accepted by all.

The energy future is undoubtedly not based on a single solution, but on a mixture of several. The  appears to be a key part for decarbonizing the most difficult sectors, such as steel production or aviation, where electricity alone is not enough. **[[Green hydrogen]]**
The transition also requires **sobriety**: consuming less and better, by insulating buildings or reducing industrial waste, often remains the most effective and least expensive lever.
Some experimental batteries work using gravity: they raise heavy concrete blocks with the day's excess solar electricity, then let them come down in the evening to produce electricity via a turbine.

The cost of solar power has fallen by 90% in fifteen years, becoming the cheapest source of electricity in history. But energy storage and the supply of rare metals remain the major challenges of the energy transition.
